scenes.title: Who is talking to your agent?

sentences.text: Contoso builds two agents this week.
The first one helps employees with I T support, inside Teams.
The second one helps customers track their orders on the company's web portal, and those customers have no Microsoft account.
In a hurry, the maker leaves both on No authentication.
One question decides whether this is fine or a disaster: who is talking to your agent?
By the end of this class you will choose the right answer for each one.
Here is the picture to keep.
Authentication is the door of a building.
You can leave the door open, so anyone walks in.
You can use the company's badge reader, so only employees get in.
Or you can fit your own lock, with keys you hand out yourself.
A wrong door either lets strangers in, or locks your real users out.
Copilot Studio gives you exactly these three doors.
The first door is No authentication.
Anyone who has the link can chat with the agent, and the agent has no idea who they are.
That can be fine for a public agent that only answers general questions.
But leaving No authentication on an agent that touches internal data is the classic mistake.
The link gets shared, and strangers now talk to an agent that knows your company's secrets.
The second door is Authenticate with Microsoft.
It is the simplest secure option, because Copilot Studio sets up Microsoft Entra I D for you automatically.
Entra I D is Microsoft's identity service, the badge reader that checks who each person is.
And in Teams the user is already identified, so they never even see a sign-in screen.
They just start chatting, and the agent knows who they are.
Now a rule the exam loves.
The Teams channel and the Microsoft three six five channel only support Authenticate with Microsoft.
Not manual authentication, and not your own provider.
So if the agent must live in Teams, the door is already chosen for you.
Keep this in mind, because the exam often hides the channel inside a long scenario and expects you to spot it.
Your turn.
The I T support agent is for Contoso employees, and it will be published in Teams.
Which authentication option should the maker choose?
Authenticate with Microsoft?
Authenticate manually with a generic OAuth two provider?
Or No authentication, since everyone in Teams is an employee anyway?
Decide before I answer.
Authenticate with Microsoft.
Teams only supports that option, and employees are signed in without ever seeing a screen.
The third door is Authenticate manually.
You use it when your users do not have a Microsoft account, for example the customers of your own web portal.
You set up an identity provider yourself, such as a generic OAuth two provider.
OAuth two is a standard that lets people sign in through an identity provider without sharing their password with your agent.
It is your own lock, with your own keys.
Once a door checks people, the agent gets variables about the user.
User dot I D identifies them.
User dot display name gives their name, so a topic can greet them.
User dot is logged in tells you whether sign-in happened.
And User dot access token holds their access token, which exists with manual authentication.
You can check in any topic which of these variables are available.
Why does all this matter?
Because identity travels with the whole conversation.
Thanks to it, the agent can look up orders for the right customer, not for somebody else.
And it can call tools with that user's own permissions, so people only reach what they are allowed to reach.
Without identity, the agent cannot tell one person from another, so it cannot protect anyone's data.
Your turn.
The order tracking agent lives on Contoso's customer portal.
Customers sign in with the portal's own accounts, and they have no Microsoft account.
Which option fits?
No authentication, because it is a public website?
Authenticate with Microsoft, because it is the simplest secure choice?
Or Authenticate manually with a generic OAuth two provider?
Decide before I answer.
Authenticate manually.
These users have no Microsoft account, so you bring your own provider.

scenes.title: Entra Agent ID: the agent's own badge

sentences.text: People have an identity, and now agents do too.
Since May twenty twenty six, when you create an agent, Copilot Studio automatically creates a Microsoft Entra Agent I D for it.
It happens when the agent is created, not when you publish it.
You cannot turn this off for an environment, and you cannot bring your own I D.
Think of it as the agent getting its own employee badge on day one.
An Agent I D is a service principal with the subtype Agent.
The OAuth sign-in flow underneath stays the same, so nothing changes for your users.
What changes is governance.
Admins can see the agent in the Microsoft Entra admin center, read its audit logs, manage its life cycle, and target its connector permissions with Conditional Access policies.
Makers find the I D in Settings, Advanced, Metadata.
Two limits to remember.
First, agents made in Agent Builder do not use app registration I Ds or Agent I Ds.
Only Copilot Studio agents get them.
Second, every Agent I D is a directory object.
So if the tenant has reached its directory object quota, the new agent cannot be created at all.
On the exam, an agent that fails to be created can point to this quota.

scenes.title: Decide: when is the badge issued?

sentences.text: Your turn.
A maker says: I will worry about the Agent I D later, it only appears when I publish.
When does Copilot Studio really create the Microsoft Entra Agent I D?
When the agent is published to its first channel?
Or when the agent is created?
Only after an admin enables it for the environment?
Decide before I answer.
When the agent is created.
It is automatic, and there is no environment opt out.
Here are the steps.
Open your agent and go to Settings.
In the Security section, select Authentication.
Choose No authentication, Authenticate with Microsoft, or Authenticate manually.
If you choose manual, fill in the OAuth two provider details.
Save your changes.
Then publish the agent, because the change only reaches the channels after you publish.
Finally, check in a topic which user variables are available.
Back to Contoso.
The I T support agent lives in Teams, so it uses Authenticate with Microsoft, and nobody sees a sign-in screen.
The customer portal agent uses Authenticate manually with OAuth two, and greets each customer by name.
Remember for the exam: Teams means Microsoft, no Microsoft account means manual, the Agent I D comes at creation, and No authentication never guards internal data.
